utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark Velesici, the military hospital, and anything else you may recognise?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the military hospital [marks], and these are Velesici [marks] behind the military hospital. This is the military hospital [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this look like the view from Colina Kapa to you, because you are familiar with the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the view from that road leading to Trebevic, where that Motel Osmice was, if that's Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Underneath the motel is Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where the motel is, so that would be it, then; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you can recognise something else -- well, to the left, to the far left, it's part of a neighbourhood. If you can recognise anything else, please mark it. Can you please mark Velesici as well? I don't think it's recorded.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] It's hidden by these greenery. This bit here is Grbavica. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you put the date and your initials?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you also see Stari Grad, that is, Bascarsija, from there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Stari Grad. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark "OC"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, with his signature and date. Yes, it was there, thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D493, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, can we get another photograph of Sarajevo, 1D2090.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, this is the transcript of the recording that is inaudible. May I have both the Serbian and English versions, and then I'll indicate which passages I want to deal with to see what Mr. Zupljanin said and what I said. And tell us, please, how 50.000 people, the population of Banja Luka, reacted to these words. 1D -- that's right, that's the Serbian. Can we have the English as well. Thank you. That's also the Serbian version. Can we get the second page in Serbian, and I believe in English as well. Do you agree that this "MS" means "Mico Stanisic"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he says -- he speaks at a ceremony of the Police Academy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Security Services Centre, Banja Luka, the occasion of the Day of the Police Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the footage that is inaudible. You are here, and the prime minister, et cetera. Could you read the passage where it says: "The first wartime conflicts ..."? In English, it's the passage which begins with the words: "On the territory of the centre ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the territory of the centre, the first war conflicts and destruction were caused by the Croatian armed forces in the bordering area with the Republic of Croatia. Innocent casualties, an exodus of Serbian refugees in Western Slavonia, fear, panic, unrest were the features of this dead-end situation in the hot August days of 1991. The CSB was in a very peculiar situation. "Being aware of the grave and complex situation in the territory we cover, and while taking all the measures to ensure that the service continue to operate in these extraordinary wartime conditions, we were desperately asking the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take steps," I suppose, "so that we could peacefully resolve certain problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this said by Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says "SZ" on the margin, and the key indicates that it's Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see these letters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. I believe it's the next page in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to read?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's not the right page. The next page in Serbian. Yes, that should be it. Let's just see where it is. It begins with the words: "I'm really glad ..." Could we get the bottom of that page back just to connect the beginning and the end of this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I'm really glad that I can emphasise here that most of the authorised officers, over 85 per cent of them, signed the solemn declaration, including a large number ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian. [In English] This part: "I'm glad that I can point out ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... including a great number of professionals of other ethnicities that remain to work in the CSB, and they are among us now."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that footage? There were 50.000 people there, the people of Banja Luka, of all ethnicities, and they all welcomed the fact that there was still quite a few policemen, Croats and Muslims, still working in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. There were members of other ethnic groups working in the CSB Banja Luka, but I can't see -- it says in the text that there was an applause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the transcript of this footage prepared by the OTP. Now, can we get the next page to see what Karadzic says, "RK." 010608, and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, after: "The UN ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To our great regret, and contrary to our will, the war has been imposed on us by part of the leadership of the two ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Down: "We regret that ..." [Interpretation] Will you please continue reading this passage and the next page in English?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "That part of them which," and then something illegible "agreement"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mutual extermination, killing and torture have been imposed on us. We are trying to participate in that as little as possible. We sometimes do not respond to fire for all of an hour, and we respond only when we are threatened."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." [Interpretation] The middle paragraph. Next page, please. But there's one passage before that: "We decided ..." or: "We have decided ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean: "We, in Bosnia-Herzegovina ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to see the top of the Serbian page, the one we had before. The Serbian page we had before, but the top of the page. [In English] "We in Bosnia and Herzegovina are not in conflict ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We decided to organise our own state." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "We decided on unilateral cease-fires." Let's see where that is in English. This is not the right page, not even in Serbian. Can we get the penultimate page in Serbian, page 5 of 6. It says "5 of 14," but it's actually 5 of 7. I hope we'll find it in English. Can we see the top of the Serbian page and the top of the English page. I probably bolded this text and then I ruined the page numbering. Can we see the next Serbian page -- sorry, the previous Serbian page. "We decided to declare unilateral ..." We read that bit. "We in Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We in Bosnia-Herzegovina are not in conflict with Croats and Muslims. We are in conflict with militant leaderships which would like to impose their own state on us, a state in which they would dominate, and we would be --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... a state in which we would be second-class citizens, and that would be accompanying people to the leading people or nation, which was clearly communicated to us during some rallies. However, Serbian people do not ask to be leaders, but will not agree to be second-rate citizens. This is the reason why we decided to organise our own state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We will never live again in someone else's state because we know what that meant before. All alien states were extremely intolerant and genocidal to us --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters haven't finished reading this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that footage of that gathering, was it the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after that Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this conciliatory tone of Stojan Zupljanin and Mico Stanisic was welcomed by the citizens? Were they met with an ovation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted? I would also tender the video-clip. It can't be heard here in the courtroom, but it is obviously audible under certain conditions, since somebody transcribed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit it. But don't forget to tender that video-clip in CD to the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D494.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe this is the last question, Minister. Allow me to remind you of the issues we have dealt in this examination. After the elections, you were both a witness and a participant to the establishment of the first democratic government. You were able to see how the parties behaved. You know that the Serbian Democratic Party delegated power to experts, and there is a difference -- a distinction between the terms "taking over power" and "assuming power," because "assuming power" means assuming power that you have won, whereas "taking over" implies taking it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember all our attempts and all the attempts of you, in the police force, to restore constitutionality and lawfulness, and all the attempts of the Serbian elite to avoid the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe during my evidence in the Stanisic case and here, I stated that in great detail and tried to explain to the Court everything that happened during 1992, especially in the police, and in 1992, when I was the minister of justice in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we get 65 ter 06147, the last exhibit. In English, it's page 107, and in Serbian -- in Serbian, it's page 107, and in English it's 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to -- well, I just want to -- it's a form of anticipatory objection. I just wondered what happened to the concept of last question. I think we need to -- we're clearly past the time allotted, and I believe that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the technical difficulties we are having, so we decided to give him five minutes more to fit into that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, this document has been admitted as Exhibit D87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the passage where it says: "Believe me ..." Do you agree that as of mid-October, the constitutional system in Bosnia-Herzegovina had collapsed completely?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many unconstitutional and illegal events and activities going on. Whether the system had collapsed, I can't say, but it's a fact that as time went by, there were more and more violations of the Constitution and the laws of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And last question: I wish to draw your attention to where it says: "Believe me ...," and so on. This is my speech of the 25th of January, my last attempt to have a joint referendum held. And what it says here, is this what was foreseen and one didn't have to be a prophet to foresee it? Let me just find where it is in English. In English, it's: "Believe me ..." Could you please read this? It's the seventh or eighth row?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Believe me, we have no influence over war or peace. Situations are very often out of control, and very often the situation is out of control. Gentlemen, all of you, including me, can picture now what would happen if, God forbid, a riot started now or an inter-ethnic and religious war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we can draw that on the board. Serbs would flee from Muslim areas, Muslims from Serb areas, and Croats would go to their areas, and there would be shooting along the way. There would be destruction of towns, there would be bloodshed, and we would find ourselves exactly where we are now; Serbs in the Serbian areas, Muslims in the Muslim areas, Croats in Croatian areas, fully homogeneous. And what would we have to do? We would again have to sit down and put three signatures on our agreement, because without all three signatures, there is no solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Minister, that unfortunately all these fears and apprehensions of mine, which I put forward before the Joint Assembly on the 25th of January, 1992, came true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think anything would have changed had we accepted a unitary Bosnia? Had the political leadership accepted a unitary Bosnia, would the people have followed us or would the same events have happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Do you agree that when the government was set up in Republika Srpska and centralisation carried out, and the government became more effective, the crime rate dropped, and that 1992 was the worst year in that respect, and that afterwards the crime rate dropped dramatically?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Minister. I believe I have exhausted my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Just one question from me, Mr. Mandic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I forgot to bring the transcript two or three days ago, and I tried to locate that from the e-court, but I couldn't. But at one point in time while you were answering the questions from Mr. Karadzic, you testified to the effect that even the military disobeyed his order, or his orders were not respected by the military. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that, Your Honours, I'm aware of that, that General Ratko Mladic did not respect the orders issued by the president of Republika Srpska or any member of the Presidency for a long period of time in the course of the war. I know that there was talk of replacing the general, dismissing him, but it was not possible at that point in time because there would have been a mutiny by the Command of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us some more concrete examples about the disobedience by the military, including General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, when Mr. Ninkovic was the minister of defence, and he hailed from Doboj, the general ordered that about a dozen ministers and members of the government administration be arrested. For ten days, they had to feed pigs in Han Pijesak, which was held by the army. President Karadzic and all the other leaders made efforts to have these people released, but the general paid no attention to them. And it was only when he decided that they should be released that they were released. So the minister of defence and some other ministers had to do labour on a military farm, on the personal orders of General Mladic, and this was contrary to all customs and the standpoint of the president, and the Presidency, and other members of the government. I find this event very telling. It illustrates the self-will of General Ratko Mladic, who did not respect the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How come General Mladic was able to retain his position, despite all this disobedience?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, and that's my personal opinion, Your Honours, the officers commanding the Army of Republika Srpska came from the former JNA, and they were suspicious of the civilian authorities, who did not come from the socialist system, but who emerged in the multi-party elections, who won the elections, and they were representatives of the various ethnic groups. So from the very beginning, there was mistrust and lack of co-operation, and no one was able to replace or dismiss General Ratko Mladic in the Republika Srpska at that time because there would have been a military coup, a military take-over, and he would have abolished all the civilian institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. That concludes your evidence. Thank you very much for your coming to the Tribunal to give it, despite all the difficulties. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you for your patience. I also wish to thank Mr. Tieger and his associates. And, Mr. President, thank you, also, and good luck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to continue, Mr. Tieger, Ms. Sutherland, with the next witness, or do you wish to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're certainly happy to continue. But we will need some time to adjust the technical aspects, log off and log back on, so the Court needs to keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if we break, we can't go until 2.30. Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's up to you, Your Honour. We'll just take a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Then we'll bring in the next witness, Mr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. He will be the 13th Prosecution witness, given that Mr. Mandic was a Court witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandilovic. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please state your name for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified before the ICTY in the Galic case on the 7th and 10th of December, 2001, in the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dragomir Milosevic case on the 17th and 18th of January, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic case on the 4th and 5th of March, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, a statement was taken from you which amalgamated evidence from your previous testimony and statements, with some additional observations as well as references to certain documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I'll proceed with the requirements of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the 24th of February, 2010, you signed an amalgamated statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would ask that 65 ter 22166 be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of page 1 of the document you can see in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you sign each page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is your signature under the witness acknowledgment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you again had an opportunity to review the statement that you signed on the 24th of February, 2010, and the exhibits that are referred to in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 3 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, there needs to be a correction to -- the word "Galic" should read "Dragomir Milosevic." And you can see in footnote 9 that it's the Dragomir Milosevic case which is footnoted, and not the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, do you wish to make two clarifications to your statement? The first was in respect to the outbreak of the war. And if we could go to page 4, please, Mr. Registrar. In paragraph 18, you describe the situations in April and May. You then state that: "Artillery shelling of the city during that period of time was far smaller than it was later on." What period are you referring to with respect to this artillery shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second clarification relates to the events which are described in paragraphs 21 to 23 of the statement. Do the events as described occur in the sequences set out in paragraphs 21 and then 22 and then 23?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me read the paragraphs. Yes, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraphs 22 and 23, you describe two incidents. Which incident occurred first in time on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can speak about these incidents only as a citizen of the city of Sarajevo, not as a member of the hospital staff, because I left the hospital on the morning of the 2nd of May. Later on, the media wrote about this event extensively, and it was broadcast on the electronic media as well. I came to understand the seriousness of the events which occurred in the morning and late afternoon of the 2nd of May. The first incident was the one at Skenderija. After that came the incident with the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the incident in relation to the 2nd Military District, did that occur before the incident at Skenderija, which is outlined in paragraph 22?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The incident with the 2nd Military District, which happened on Skenderija Street, was after this. It was the day after, because these things happened on the 2nd of May when, in the afternoon, President Izetbegovic was stopped at Butmir Airport in Sarajevo, and on the following day there was an exchange between President Izetbegovic and the Command of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know what street that occurred on, that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the incident that occurred in relation to the column of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. We can see from paragraph 23 that you say that that incident took place in Vojvode Stepe Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that refers to the first incident, the one that happened on the 2nd of May. That did take place in that street which we referred to in Sarajevo as "on the bank." The second incident was a day later in Skenderija Street, when units of the 2nd Military District were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we have the event that's described in paragraph 23 as happening first in time on the 2nd of May, and then we have the incident --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- which is described in paragraph 22 happening second in time on the 2nd of May, and the event which is described in paragraph 21 happening the following day, on the 3rd of May; is that correct? Do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So with that correction to paragraph 6 of your statement and the two clarifications that we have just made now in relation to paragraph 18 and paragraphs 21 to 23, do you confirm that your amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked, under oath, about these topics today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I seek to have the amalgamated witness statement, 65 ter 22166, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to a public version of this witness statement, the Prosecution intends to redact from pages 24 to 26 references to those documents which will be admitted under seal; that is, the associated exhibits listed in Confidential Appendix B to the Rule 92 ter notification which was filed, which will be discussed at the completion of the evidence-in-chief. That is, in the table, it is documents numbered 8 to 15 and 18 to 20 of paragraph 118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is my understanding that you are seeking to put under seal 12 documents, but I wanted to clarify what reasons are behind it. So we'll come to that later, when you deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I'll now read a brief statement -- a brief summary of the witness's evidence. Dr. Mandilovic was born in Serbia. In 1975, he qualified as a doctor of medicine, graduating from the Faculty of Medicine in Sarajevo. In 1986, he became an ear, nose, and throat specialist. After becoming a medical doctor in 1975, he completed compulsory military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Between 1978 and 1982, he was a major at the Sarajevo Garrison Infirmary. From 1982, he worked at the Military Hospital in Sarajevo, which was renamed the State Hospital in May 1992, and remained working there throughout the course of the war, 1992 to 1995. He continues to work at the hospital, which is now named the Sarajevo General Hospital. Dr. Mandilovic describes the conditions of work at the hospital during the war. Day-to-day life was terrible. They experienced shelling, small-arms fire, water shortages, drug and oxygen shortages, food shortages, and power cuts. Dr. Mandilovic describes how, in the winter of 1992 to 1993, the supply of fuel, electricity, and water was greatly reduced, which were all vital for the normal functioning of the hospital. Conditions were also very hard from late 1993 into early 1994. Dr. Mandilovic describes how the hospital building was directly hit on several occasions with certain types of projectiles so that the facade of the hospital, the window frames and glass, were all damaged and destroyed. The southern side of the hospital received the most damage. The hospital received thousands of hits from small-arms fire, and window-panes on the building were shattered. A number of people in the hospital were hit by sniper fire during the war, and a number of hospital patients and staff were wounded in the hospital. Dr. Mandilovic describes how the shelling was so intense that the wards had to be set up in the basement. During certain periods of heavy shelling, all the patients would be taken down to the ground floor. Shells landed on several occasions whilst casualties were arriving at the hospital. During the course of the war, Dr. Mandilovic constantly treated casualties both from sniping and from mortar projectiles, and their dispersive effects. He performed surgery on wounded patients on a daily basis from September 1992 through 1994. Dr. Mandilovic describes how the shelling created obstacles to the work of the hospital, both in physical and psychological terms, and how immensely stressful it was working and operating on patients under these conditions. He and his colleagues experienced constant fear as they went about their work in the hospital, and patients suffered from re-traumatisation. Dr. Mandilovic describes how the attacks on the civilians were designed to instill terror in the civilian population, and by denying the hospital the supplies necessary and by making life more difficult by shelling the hospital, the terror effect on the population was increased. Dr. Mandilovic was on duty in the State Hospital on the 28th of August, 1995, and treated casualties from scheduled shelling incident G19, known as the Markale II incident. Some 40 people were brought into the State hospital, most of them civilians. It was clear to the witness that the injuries of the casualties were caused by shell shrapnel. Dr. Mandilovic authenticates selected hospital records relating to scheduled sniping incidents F4, F11, F14, and F15, and scheduled shelling incidents G4, G6, G7, G8, G9, G10, G13, and G19. That concludes the brief summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, I now will ask you a few questions in relation to the contents of your statement. You described in your statement the shelling and sniping of the hospital. And for the Court and the accused, this is paragraphs 42 to 58. You said that the hospital building was subject to sniper fire and was shelled on several occasions. From which direction was the hospital hit by shells and sniper fire? Direction or directions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Those were two questions. I have to make a small correction. The hospital was shelled for 44 months throughout the conflict. I have to note that the intensity of the shelling varied in different time-periods; that it was physically hit the most from the southern side, the hospital, I mean. However, it was also hit from the northern side and also from the eastern side. In a word, that means that the hospital was hit from all sides over those 44 months of war, but the shelling that was the most intensive was on the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from the southern side of the hospital, what is -- what is directly in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The hospital had the misfortune of -- I can say that quite freely now -- of being on the very front-line. Miljacka is right across Marin Dvor, and then after the Miljacka River are the first slopes of Trebevic, where the Jewish cemetery is. The Jewish cemetery was a target of the Bosnian Serb soldiers throughout the war. They controlled the area of Marin Dvor and the area of the hospital, therefore, from there throughout the war. The Jewish cemetery is very close to the hospital, and, therefore, I can state quite freely that this is one of the few hospitals of that size, importance, and capacity that was ever on a front-line throughout the history of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any other areas from where the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I said a few moments ago that we were hit from the north as well -- from the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the southern side -- was there any other areas where the shelling was coming from in relation to the southern side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that wouldn't be possible. It came from the south. Now, "the south" is a broad notion. It is the south-west and the south-east. However, you could not be hit on the southern side if the shelling came from the north. That is pure physics, it is the laws of physics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Mandilovic, I haven't been clear. In relation to shells that were landing on the southern side, you mentioned already the Jewish cemetery. Were there any other areas, across the river where the Jewish cemetery was or elsewhere, where shells were being projected from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I firmly believe that. I firmly believe that, because that entire side was under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces. It's the area of Vraca and Grbavica, in addition to the Jewish cemetery. And immediately above the Jewish cemetery was Trebevic, which was also under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces. So throughout the war, we referred to the Jewish cemetery as a very prominent location, close to Marin Dvor and the hospital. However, in addition to that, there were other active points that probably had some heavy weaponry as well. If I may, I'd like to be very specific and to correct something. We should not believe that the Jewish cemetery was the only point from which the hospital and the rest of town were targeted. It was just the closest point to the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I wish to now focus on hospital medical records from the State Hospital and another health institution. Dr. Mandilovic, you stated in paragraph 116 of your statement that you had occasion to see medical records from the Sarajevo University Clinic Centre and the Forensic Institute of the Faculty of Medicine in Sarajevo, which is the same institution of the Kosevo Hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like you to look at a couple of documents. And I would ask that we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, can you describe for the Court the working conditions in the hospital just briefly? Because you do -- they are contained throughout your statement, but I would just like to you briefly describe for the Chamber what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, throughout the war, conditions were very difficult. We had a constant shortage of medicine, medical material, and energy, power as well, water, and there was no gas either. So all these elements that are very important for the normal functioning of a hospital were at reduced level. We had to be very careful about using the resources we had. We had to save our resources, and the number of wounded and ill persons was on the rise all the time. Therefore, the situation was very difficult. However, I have to say that thanks to our management, the hospital that was on the front-line worked 'round the clock, 24 hours a day, over 44 months. Not at a single point in time did the hospital grind to a halt. It was always in a position to help wounded and ill persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all of the other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We fought with all these difficulties. We created new doctrines, as it were. We were compelled to do so. However, as we look at our results today, we see that we were absolutely successful. We did receive certain assistance from humanitarian organisations, from the Red Cross, but in conditions of war, you never get enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe the day-to-day life --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe what day-to-day life was like in Sarajevo throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can, yes. Life in the hospital, working in the hospital, it ran along parallel lines with life in town, itself, and that was manifested in the following. Ordinary citizens of Sarajevo were the victims of terror every day, terror inflicted by heavy weaponry from the hills surrounding Sarajevo. Also, they did not have vital things; water, electricity, gas, and food, of course. All of that seriously threatened the life of the population. Also, it impaired their health. In view of how long it went on, we have many people in Sarajevo who were there throughout the war and who suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder, not only members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but all citizens of Sarajevo, who can say that they were together with the soldiers at the front-line. That would be a proper statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides the post-traumatic stress disorder that you have just mentioned, what else did you observe in relation to the mental and emotional effects that the shelling and sniping had on the civilian population in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not the most competent person for taking part in this kind of a discussion, but it is certain that the citizens who spent the war in Sarajevo were affected by it. You can see that through their nervousness, the rush they seemed to be in all the time. In traffic, you see how easily they flare up. You see that this is not exactly normal behaviour. When you go to other towns in the region, the population seems quite different and they communicate with other people in a different way, and amongst themselves, too. Obviously, this long siege of 44 months has certain repercussions, not only in terms of the physical condition of the citizens of Sarajevo, but also their psychological structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What psychological or physical injuries do you suffer from as a result of the shelling and sniping campaign which occurred in Sarajevo from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I personally think that I have not been affected, but somebody else would have to say. People always think of themselves as being completely healthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mandilovic. That completes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish to deal now with the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question is: One of the associated exhibits is a video-clip, the number of which is 65 ter -- the 65 ter number of which is 40292?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is of a duration of two hours, six minutes, but my understanding is the witness only referred to the 50-second excerpt from the video. So only that part will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then you will provide only that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, with the clip, Your Honour, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any other observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we don't have any objections to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will admit all the associated exhibits, as discussed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, it's now your witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will try to put as few questions as possible, or, rather, as many questions as possible which can be answered by a yes or no. Did we know each other before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your wife Aida -- is your wife, Aida, a dentist in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are an active-duty soldier, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm waiting for the translation. What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The last rank I held was that of major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, you probably must have heard this, but we are hearing the interpreter's interpretation. Because both of you are speaking the same language, please put a pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did your active military service end, and how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did you work in the Military Hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: For 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did your active service in the military end?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I left the hospital on the morning of the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did your active military service end by the simple act of leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the former JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you leave the Military Hospital on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I left the Military Hospital because the former JNA was no longer the army of Yugoslavia, it was not the army of the Yugoslav nation's nationalities. Practically 1991, when Slovenia seceded, after that Croatia and then Bosnia-Herzegovina, it stopped being the JNA. It completely changed its ideology, it completely changed its doctrine, it completely changed its command staff, and it completely changed its insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did it change its insignia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 or 1992. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That it changed its insignia before you left the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. You know what the insignia and flags of the JNA were, and you know that they changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I only asked whether it happened before you left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is absolutely yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll show that in the course of the proceedings. Why did you leave the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Because I disagreed with the situation as it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, there are two aspects of this. One is leaving the army, and the other one is leaving the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in one place you wrote that you returned in order to work because you couldn't abandon your patients, and yet you say that it's one and the same now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the hospital on the day when it changed its name and its purpose, which was after the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the owner of the Military Hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the 10th of May, 1992, it was part of the JNA, or the former JNA. From the point of time when Yugoslavia disintegrated, it became the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did it stop being the property of the JNA, and how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It stopped being the property of the former JNA on the 10th of May, 1992, when those people who did not want to remain left, and the hospital then changed its name and its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did it also change its owner? Does ownership of property change in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's a legal issue. But there's one thing you should know. As of March, Bosnia-Herzegovina was an independent state. Its flag was flown before the UN on the East River. It was recognised. So from that point on, the JNA was on foreign territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that is also a legal issue, but my first question referred to the elementary property rights. But you feel that on the 10th of May, with the entry of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, legal ownership of the hospital ceased?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are trying to involve me in legal questions. I cannot answer those. But there's another question I can answer, and that is that: On the 10th of May, it was not the Patriotic League and the Green Berets that entered the hospital, but the regular Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can tell you that the take-over of the Military Hospital was negotiated by the minister of the interior directly, so we can't talk about Green Berets here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I didn't object earlier when Mr. Karadzic said that the witness stated at some point that the reason why he didn't want to leave the hospital was because of his patients, because I knew that it was in paragraph 25. However, in future, when Mr. Karadzic puts something to the witness that he says, I would like him to provide the source of either the transcript or the statement so that the witness has some idea. For example, when he says: "But you feel on the 10th of May, with the entry of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, legal ownership of the hospital ceased?" I don't think the witness ever said that, so I would like him to take me to the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Bearing that in mind, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But the witness just said a little while ago that the Military Hospital ceased being military property of the JNA on the 10th of May, so that's what I was referring to. I don't need to refer to something he said previously. Let me just gather my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, are you saying that the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were not the regular armed units of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about those relations. In my view, the regular armed forces were the Territorial Defence and the MUP, the reserve force of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that the Military Hospital, starting in April or even in late March, was completely encircled by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can only partially accept what you say. I said that in my statement, I noticed that in April there were groups of men in the vicinity of the hospital who had not been there before, but they were not armed and they did not prevent anyone from going into or out of the hospital. They did not check anyone's identity papers. It was a very soft, barely noticeable encirclement. I might even not have noticed it had those not been times when tensions were high and people were under stress, so they observed things like that. What forces those were, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they wearing mostly civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who fired shots on the Military Hospital before the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say. On the 2nd of March [as interpreted], I left the hospital, so I couldn't say, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who fired shots at the hospital in April, before the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: If there was any shooting, I didn't notice it, really. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I think there's a mistake in the transcript. It says: "On the 2nd of March, I left the hospital." I think that's supposed to be "2nd of May."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D2104. 1D2104. 1D2104, this is not it. No, that's not the document. "SAO34061" is the number on the document. Can we put this on the ELMO until we see what's wrong with the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up to the 2nd of May, you were in the hospital, the Military Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, we have the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do we have a translation, Your Honour? I can't read B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we don't have a translation yet. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, may I ask you to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, you couldn't have seen it because it's strictly confidential. But who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: What it says here is "The Command of the 2nd Military District, Operations Duty Team, Strictly Confidential Number," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read out the part that's been highlighted: "On the territory ..."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Only what's highlighted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: "On the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are still ongoing activities on the arming and strengthening of forces of the Territorial Defence. There are more and more open provocations and attacks on members of the JNA and facilities. "Paramilitary units have been especially active in Sarajevo, where there are open conflicts and settling of accounts, and there have been attacks on the Military Hospital in Sarajevo and setting up of barricades all over the city, with a view to preventing movement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there were provocations and attacks on members of the JNA and its facilities? This is dated the 21st of April, so by that date, these things had already started?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there were provocations. I can believe that because there were very many military facilities and the barracks in Sarajevo. There was a big military academy and so on, so that it's possible that there were provocations. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Doctor. I think we have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Reid will e-mail it to the Defence and they can upload the document into e-court. And they can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, while we are waiting: Did you have a neuropsychology ward in the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What floor was it on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The third and fourth floors of the right block, the block near the railway station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 2. Just let everybody see the front page first. What we read out is the second half of the section entitled "The Enemy." Now, can we have page 2, page 2 of the Serbian version, in e-court, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read where it says: "In the town, throughout the day ..." And in the English version, it's -- I think it's the passage beginning with: "The fighting has been going on all day ..." Can you read the second paragraph from the top, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: "At 0655 hours, the Sarajevo Military Hospital was hit by a mortar shell. The dining-room on the fourth floor of the Neuropsychiatry Ward was hit."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading slowly for the sake of the interpreters: "There was no casualties; only material damage. At 735 hours in the morning, the Military Hospital was hit again by two stray bullets, which broke the windows in one of the hospital rooms. One patient was cut by broken glass. In addition to that, the paramilitary formations have been laying siege to the Sarajevo Military Hospital all day long, and an attack on it is to be expected."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 4 in the Serbian language, please, so that the witness can see the signature and the source. [In English] In English, you can put the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the usual stamp of receipt?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the usual one. I don't know the colonel in question, but the form is typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, how come you don't know about this shelling and this shell that fell into the Neuropsychiatry Ward on the fourth floor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about it. I worked far away from there. I worked on the 12th floor of the main building, so I really don't know about this. I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: However, may I say something else, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I disagree with this statement. I absolutely disagree with this statement that the hospital was surrounded by some patriotic forces and that they were awaiting the attack on the hospital. I repeat, once again, people normally walked in, walked out. There were no major movements there. Anyone could leave the hospital whenever they wanted to. There were no special restrictions imposed. I think that this is an exaggerated report. It's a bit exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say, Doctor, that the strictly confidential report of the Command of the 2nd Military District to the General Staff of Yugoslavia was a false one for some reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying it was false. I just said it was exaggerated. That's for sure. I'm talking about my impressions in the said period, and I cannot deny what was the case. There was evident freedom of movement; no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say, Doctor, that your impression is more accurate than the assessment of the Command of the 2nd Military District in relation to the security of its facilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Mandilovic: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from being asked and answered, Your Honour, it's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D495, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Wouldn't this normally be MFI'd? Do we have the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We were offered the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 61, you said that in -- no, no, page 61, today's transcript. You said that in Dobrovoljacka Street, an exchange had taken place, the president of the Presidency, Izetbegovic, and the Command of the 2nd Military District. Did that happen by accident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: By accident. That was not an exchange at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: What happened is what everybody knows about, that this convoy of the 2nd Military District was moving down Dobrovoljacka Street, and President Izetbegovic was in one of the APCs. There was supposed to be an exchange. President Izetbegovic was supposed to go to the Presidency, and General Kukanjac was supposed to go to the west, to Lukavica. That was the deal, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was the agreement that was reached in the presence of General MacKenzie or, rather, the UN?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Izetbegovic, at Skenderija, turned towards the Presidency, what happened to the rest of the convoy that hadn't left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened because I wasn't present, you know. I just know what all other citizens of Sarajevo know from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the citizens of Eastern Sarajevo as well or are you referring only to this other part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I mean all the citizens who followed the media at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As an officer, as a member of that army at that point in time, can you tell us what it was that happened? The Trial Chamber doesn't know. A lot of things go without saying for the two of us because we are from there, but the Trial Chamber doesn't know about a great many things that haven't been presented to them yet.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this convoy was cut off and there was a skirmish of sorts, and a number of members of the former JNA were killed. That is what is known with regard to that day. That was presented in public. It was in all the media, it was on TV. I think that that is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were a number of soldiers and officers killed, and were others taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were some deaths in that operation. Also, some members of the former JNA were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that an incident that Ejub Ganic, a member of the Presidency, was accused of? According to those criminal charges, he was in charge of that attack, and is he not in Great Britain now, awaiting extradition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the media say, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 2nd of May, a day before that, there were attacks and there were casualties. Am I right when I say that a lot before the 2nd of May, there were attacks by the Green Berets at the Command of the 2nd Military District in Bistrik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It is hard to say whether it was the Green Berets or somebody else, but there were tensions. I was not present there, but, again, people talked and the media reported about this. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were attacks and that there were deaths?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 1st and 2nd of May, the JNA Centre, Dom Una, that was a cultural centre and so on, was it not under a blockade of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Units of the Territorial Defence answered -- entered the JNA Centre. How, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that at one point in time, representatives of the JNA came to the Military Hospital, one unit came. Do you agree that this was the protective regiment that had come to guard the Military Hospital, not to observe the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct. I said that on several occasions. Sometime toward the end of April, about 20 members of the former JNA came. They were withdrawing from Zagreb, from Croatia. These young men, specifically, were at Zagreb Airport, Pleso, providing security there. They came to our institution, accompanied by an officer and an NCO. They were deployed on the 12th floor, on the eastern and western balcony, and some of them were close to the gate. It was hard to say what their proper function was. If it was for the sake of protection, there were too few of them. If they were observers, then that was quite proper. It is hard for me to say what their function was, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the orders they received were to assist the team at the JNA Centre and that they went there in an ambulance and two Pinzgauers or something like that, open vehicles, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not see that, but again, I heard people talk about it and I saw it on TV, yes. Those were the men, the young men, who were led by their officers. They left the hospital compound where they were parked and they went to town. I really don't know what their intention was or what their function was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at the bridge on the Miljacka, on the one side is Skenderija and on the other side is the Presidency, is it correct that they were attacked there and that both they and their vehicles burned? We have photographs to prove that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. These photographs were reported in the media. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct -- actually, I'd like to -- well, just a moment, please. I don't know if the other side and the Trial Chamber will agree that we admit a statement -- a witness statement given before the police of Republika Srpska about these incidents, or should I simply quote from that document and ask the witness for his position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can put the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement made by Dr. Tausan. Do you know Dr. Tomislav Tausan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: He was the director of the Military Hospital in Sarajevo up until the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew him personally; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You addressed him on the 2nd of May, and you said that you would leave the JNA. And he was not opposed to that. It was a proper conversation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I talked to him earlier on. Dr. Tausan was very co-operative in that point of time. Whoever wanted to leave the hospital had his absolute approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He says in his statement that already from the 5th of April onwards, from that big rally that was held before the Assembly, he saw masses of participants in the rally from the neighbouring buildings, and he said that members of Juka Prazina's unit opened fire and that the gun-shots reached the Military Hospital as well. He says: "From that day, Muslims fired at facilities in the Military Hospital from time to time, so the command sent a group of soldiers to help provide security for the hospital. And I remember that there was a total of 26 soldiers who were providing security. One of the stronger sniper attacks came from the Unis building. So within the compound of the hospital, no one dared move about." Do you know where these Unis buildings are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I know where the Unis buildings are, of course I do. They are close to the hospital. However, I don't know how come Dr. Tausan has this information that these were Juka Prazina's units. It could have been any unit. It could have been absolutely any other unit in that chaos that prevailed in town. I don't know how come he is so sure that it was Juka Prazina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the headquarters of a particular unit were in that building, and that gun-fire came from these Unis skyscrapers, and that the target was even the compound of the Military Hospital, as your director says?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That may have been the case, but perhaps that was after the 2nd of May, when I was no longer in that hospital. However, as far as I can remember, no one was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says here: "The first more serious attack against the Military Hospital was on the 6th of April, 1992. That is when over 1.000 Muslims moved towards the hospital from the police building. However, when they saw that the security detail of the hospital would offer resistance, they gave up." Afterwards, he says: "There was a sniper from a Magribija mosque that was operating all the time." Do you know where that mosque is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: First I wish to respond to your first question, which is actually a statement, not a question. There is a reference to 1.000 Muslim men. Do you think that 26 men who had come from Pleso Airport can really defend a hospital from 1.000 men? That's ridiculous. And of course I know where the mosque is. It's below the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, did you have something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to object to the compound question: "Do you agree that the headquarters of a particular unit were in that building, and that the gun-fire came from that building, and that the target was even the compound ..." It's three questions all rolled into one, so I would just ask Dr. Karadzic if he could ask single questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic. You understand the intervention of Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you. Dr. Mandilovic knows what stuffed cabbage is on our national menu. You fold a lot of things into one leaf of cabbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, whether a group of 1.000 disorganised and untrained soldiers could be deterred by 26 trained and equipped soldiers is a different matter, but let me read on: "One of the fiercest attacks on the Military Hospital was on the 26th of April, but thankfully without any losses." Do you remember that sniper attack at the Military Hospital the 26th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. You have to understand that in Sarajevo, throughout April, and especially by night, there were bursts of gun-fire, automatic and single shots, all the time, but you could never tell where it was directed. So it could have happened, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say you only heard the sound, you couldn't tell the direction, but could you tell where it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I really don't know. At that time, I was not in a position to be targeted by anyone. On the floor where I was working, there was no damage. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then he goes on to say: "In one of the worst attacks on the Military Hospital on the 3rd of May, two patients were wounded. They notified the UNPROFOR and complained about the situation." But by that time, you had already left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, when you returned, were you informed about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that anyone told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, based on what you said on page 63 of today's transcript, and later also, that there was no electricity, water, gas, and many other things, but when there was electricity, water, and gas, and other supplies, where did these supplies come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: From the city infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when you speak about Sarajevo and the citizens of Sarajevo, is that meant to include the Serb citizens of Sarajevo, both those under the control of Muslim authorities and those in Grbavica, under Serb control, and in Lukavica, Vraca, and other areas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely include all the citizens of Sarajevo. I don't divide it in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that all these traumas and all the hardships in Sarajevo also were suffered by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, the citizens experienced limited hardships. You mustn't forget that for 44 months, the city was besieged. Everything was in short supply, and the citizens of Sarajevo lived from one day to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is it the case that there were around 300.000 Muslims in that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say; not because I don't want to say before this Court, but because I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all this population, regardless of their affiliation, received all their water from wells in the Serb territory, Ilidza and other sources?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. That goes without saying. That's the physical order of things. Water comes from elevations downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And before this tunnel was opened, most of the power supply came from Vogosca and through other Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
