utterances.text: I agree with only one thing, Mr. Karadzic. Everything that came from the territory controlled by Bosnian Serbs was insufficient and hard to come by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it was hard to come by because of whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When my learned friend, Ms. Sutherland, said that you mentioned the Jewish cemetery as a source of fire, and then you said that entire side was under Serb control, you said, I firmly believe, and you also said, Probably. From what part of the Jewish cemetery did the gun-fire come from, from the west or the east?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know from which side, but it certainly came from the Jewish cemetery, among other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that from one side, from the west side -- on the west side of the Jewish cemetery, there were Serbs, and on the east side, the territory of the cemetery, itself, was no-man's land?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the tactical commander in that area. What you're telling me now is something I didn't know before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if you had known that on the border of the Jewish cemetery facing the old town, there were Muslims, how would you then have identified the source of fire? Now when I tell you that this is a fact, what would you say? Who was firing, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In our minds, there was no question who was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean those were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the military forces of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: We know because we followed -- we watched where the fire was coming from. You see, Sarajevo -- and the honourable Court maybe doesn't know this, but Sarajevo is laid out in a very peculiar way. It's in a -- lies in a depression. It's surrounded by hills. The diametre from north to south is very small, and it is elongated along the east-west line. And the part of Sarajevo where the hospital is is such that the distance between the hospital and the positions held by Bosnian Serbs is very small, so you could hear the shot fired on the hill, and after a few seconds you would hear the explosion on the target where the shell landed. I'm sorry. In one of my statements, I even said that approximately the Jewish cemetery is about 400 metres away from the hospital, as the crow flies, of course, so good observers had absolutely no trouble discerning where the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what would have been the interests of Serbs to fire at the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: There could be more than one interest. The first and main purpose was to destabilise the whole city, to destabilise and destroy all the vital functions of the city. Health-care is an important function that significantly affects the morale of people, and I believe that is one of the main reasons for the permanent fire in the attempts to stop the hospital from operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: How do I know what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you've just said. How do you know about these Serbian purposes and objectives for firing on the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: What else could it be? Why did you keep the city of Sarajevo for 44 months in this horrible siege? If that was not your purpose, you would have let the city of Sarajevo live normally, you would have allowed it to communicate with the outside world. You surrounded the city, held it under 44 -- for 44 months under fierce fire in terror for that purpose, and the hospital was a vital part of the city life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please, would you only tell us about things you know. Who then fired on the 10th of May -- up to the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was following that exchange closely, so I think that's an unfair criticism. Dr. Karadzic asked -- he solicited the answer. The witness provided it. He then asked, Well, how do you know? The witness explained. The witness is clearly answered the questions he has been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I fully agree. The Chamber agrees with you. Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was then opening fire on the Military Hospital before the 10th of May? Who, for instance, on the 2nd of May started an attack at the Military Hospital? Were those joint units of the Territorial Defence, the BH, the Patriotic League, Green Berets, infantry, weapons, snipers, and all the other available assets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. You know that from the morning of the 2nd of May, I was not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of May was a very important day in the history of the city of Sarajevo, and a very important day in the conflict, itself. So that attack, if it happened, it was overshadowed by much larger events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know and were you informed that on the 3rd of May, there was fire on the Military Hospital from the building of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a Browning, rockets, and an anti-aircraft gun, and the seventh and eighth floors of the hospital were hit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The Assembly building was held by the Territorial Defence, and they certainly didn't shoot at a building that would eventually end up in their hands. I don't believe that, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave aside belief or disbelief.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say "I believe," because I wasn't there, I didn't see, so I have to make a reservation to whatever I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to what I originally asked. If a shell was targeting a military hospital, or a round from an infantry weapon, if it's coming from the south side, from the hills, that means to you that the Serbs are shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you came back, was there any damage on the Military Hospital, on the facade, or inside, in the Psychiatric Ward, et cetera, that you could see when you came back on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Minor damage, absolutely minor damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Debelo Brdo is, Debelo Hill?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it's south of the hospital. I couldn't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who controlled Debelo Brdo? Whose forces were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If somebody's shooting from that hill, Debelo Brdo, at the hospital, what would you conclude?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say, because I don't know where Debelo Brdo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if someone is shooting from the Jewish cemetery, how do you know whether it's from the western or the eastern edge of the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why do you then blame it on the Serbs, when it could have been the Muslims equally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the logic. Why would the Muslims shoot at their own territory? It's very illogical. That's one. And, second, that begs the issue where the Muslim side would have taken the weapons and the ammunition. Where would they have taken heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to tell me, as a major, that the Muslim side, in the east of Sarajevo, had no tanks, no Howitzers, no recoilless guns, no rocket-launchers, no heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Heavy weapons, I did not see. They had light weapons that I could see in very small amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That you could see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You referred to mental and emotional consequences of the 44-month-long war against Sarajevo. What is your psychiatric training, actually?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of a general practitioner. But if you read that transcript carefully, I said at the beginning that I'm not an expert in the field and that I'm only stating my impressions as a human being with a small import of medical training. I qualified that statement very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't find it now, but did you mention that there were many injuries from hand-grenades in people who came to see you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I never, never mentioned hand-grenades. I only mentioned mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: [In English] "... a number of casualties started to arrive. They were mainly civilians." [Interpretation] That's what you said in the Galic case. But then I suppose it should have been mentioned in the Milosevic case. But it says: "Galic, December 2001, page 1075, lines 4 through 6." How did you know who was civilian and who was a soldier? Because you said, yourself, that many people did not have uniforms and fought in their own clothes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The way we knew was because the first ID cards were then issued for members of the Territorial Defence, and the injured would come, accompanied by medical personnel or their own friends, and we would write down their names, their age, and their affiliation, if any, to a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Abdulah Nakas, on the 10th of May, left the Military Hospital and went to Sokolac with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That is erroneous information, it's mis-information. I saw, from the previous documents, that you have excellent intelligence, so I'm surprised someone told you that. Dr. Nakas attended a military exercise in March with the units of the former JNA, but after that he came back to the hospital very quickly. He was in the hospital, and he participated actively in the hand-over of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Bakir or Abdulah Nakas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: They were both there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say he did not leave the Military Hospital with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: You are getting the time mixed up. I'm referring to May. In May, Dr. Abdulah Nakas was in the hospital and didn't leave it with the remains of the former JNA. So you have the wrong information there, completely wrong. Dr. Nakas, I remember it was March when he attended a military exercise, some military manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how far from the Military Hospital is the Catholic Church at Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The Catholic Church? It's perhaps 200 or 300 metres, as the crow flies, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Monday, we will look at some maps and photographs, but do you know that the Green Berets placed -- or, rather, located their logistics base next to the Catholic Church at Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Military Hospital was shot at from the north. Who could have fired shots at the Military Hospital from the north?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did say that, and you can see the damage to this day. There were some shells which landed from the north side. I've been saying all the time that the city of Sarajevo was surrounded on all sides, so that on the north side, projectiles were fired from the positions of the Bosnian Serbs and hit the hospital, the facade, the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that these shells might have been fired from Poljine, and that between Poljine and the Military Hospital, there were no weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Poljine is an area in the northern part of the city of Sarajevo. It was under the control of the Bosnian Serbs. That area is quite suitable for the deployment of artillery pieces, so I thought that the shells had arrived from there. But, of course, I cannot verify that. I wasn't there at the time, but projectiles did come from the north side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility that between Poljine and the Military Hospital at Kosevsko Brdo, Ciglana, Crni Vrh, there were installations and firing positions of the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "installations," that sounds like something very sophisticated. I think that the forces of the Territorial Defence never had artillery pieces requiring installations, especially not at the beginning of the war. So I really don't think that they were the ones firing on the hospital. They didn't have the weapons to do that, nor would it have been in their interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's another question, Doctor. My first question is: At Kosevsko Brdo, which is right behind the Military Hospital, behind Crni Vrh, was there a position of the Muslim Army, a staff, mortars, a tank in a tunnel, and so on; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but you should ask UNPROFOR for that information and the European Observers. They would be the ones to tell you that. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll look at the pictures tomorrow [as interpreted], but is Kosevsko Brdo and the tunnel and Ciglane, are these much closer to the Military Hospital than Poljine is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Crni Vrh right behind the hospital, in the direction of the north?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what the Military Hospital was hit with and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The State Hospital was hit from all sorts of artillery pieces in the course of the war; infantry weapons and artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you're a major. What artillery pieces, and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not at the firing positions, but I'm sure they were 80- or 120-millimetre mortars, anti-aircraft machine-guns and anti-aircraft guns. As regards infantry weapons, we needn't even mention those, because the artillery pieces were much worse. And this happened from May 1992 until the beginning of the negotiations in Dayton, and even during the negotiations in Dayton there were certain breaches of the cease-fire. So throughout the time when Sarajevo was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, are you saying that anti-aircraft machine-guns, and anti-aircraft guns, and mortars are artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that anti-aircraft machine-guns and guns are, but mortars are, as are cannons, Howitzers, and other artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the damage on the hospital from this heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The damage was enormous. You can see that on the pictures, especially the southern facade of the hospital. It wasn't just the facade that was damaged, but the rooms inside. The entire south side was completely unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On all the floors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on all the floors. You can see that on the photographs. I looked at the photographs when testifying previously before the Tribunal, but I have to say I'm not really happy with them. These are photographs taken in 1993, showing damage, but I wish you had photographs from 1995 so the Court could see the extent of the damage then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Dr. Bakir Nakas wrong, then, when he said that the first seven floors were safe because they were protected by the surrounding buildings, while you said there was no protection? Which of you two is right? He said the first seven floors were safe, while you say that none of the floors were safe.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bakir Nakas couldn't have said anything like that. He was our chief manager in the war. He deserves a lot of credit for the existence and work of the hospital. He couldn't have said anything like that. He toured the hospital every day and saw the effects of the shelling, so I have no doubt that -- he couldn't have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop there. Before we conclude, there's one matter to deal with in private session. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise for today. We'll resume on Monday, 1.30. Is it correct that we'll continue with this witness, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that was the projection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So probably you must have heard from the Victims and Witnesses Section, Dr. Mandilovic, until your cross-examination is over, you are not supposed to discuss your evidence with anybody else. I hope you have a refreshing and good, nice weekend. I'll see you all on Monday at 1.30. I have to -- I'd like to thank all the staff members who kindly agreed to sit at 1.30 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of July, 2010, at 1.30 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.32 p.m.,
